d: One looks along the ship to the starboard, beyond the board to the sea and the horizon. Around the main mast in the middle is sea people, busy with dews, stored; beyond them one keeps knights and squires on the starboard board, also stored; from them a little distant Tristan, standing with entangled arms and looking in the sea, looking at him at feet, sluggishly stored, Kurwenal. From the mast, from the height, one hears again the voice of the young sailor
Isolde and Brangeane alone, with completely closed curtains. Isolde rises up with disparaging rage gestures. Brangeue falls at her feet
Through the curtains enters Kurwenal with impetuousness

Kurwenal goes back. Brangäne, hardly her powerful, turns into the background. Isolde, summarizing her whole feeling for the decision, slowly steps towards the bed of rest with a great attitude, on whose head she leans firmly towards the entrance. --- Tristan enters and remains reverently at the entrance. --- Isolde has sunk into his sight with terrible excitement.--- Long silence

Garden with tall trees in front of the chamber of Isoldes, to which steps, lying sideways, lead up. Bright, graceful summer night. At the open door a burning torch is put on. Hunting dung. Brangäne, on the steps of the chamber, looks after the ever-removable hunting dung. She looks anxiously back into the chamber, in which she sees Isolde near. To it steps out of the chamber, fiery moving, Isolde

Castle garden. On one side high castle buildings, on the other side a low wall armor, interrupted by a waiting; in the background the castle gate. The position can be assumed on rocky height; through openings one looks at a wide sea horizon. The whole makes the impression of the lordlessness, poorly cared for, here and there damaged and overgrown. In the foreground, on the inner side, lies Tristan, under the shadow of a large linden tree, sleeping on a resting bed, as lifelessly stretched out. At the head of it sits Kurwenal, bent in pain over him and carefully listening to his breath. From the outside one hears, when the curtain is raised, a shepherd's rowing, longingly and sadly blown on a shawl. --- The shepherd appears himself with the upper body above the wall armor and looks in part

Kurwenal had immediately returned behind Isolde; speechless in a terrible shock he attended the performance and stared motionlessly at Tristan. From the depth one hears now dull murmuring and gun-climbing. The shepherd comes up over the wall
